claims.text: Interface-driven dislocation climb is the dominant creep mechanism in nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers under prolonged elevated-temperature stress.
Local short-range ordering near interphase boundaries facilitates and spatially modulates dislocation climb.
Dislocations climb and rearrange preferentially at FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
Interfacial short-range order governs deformation through its effect on the distribution of antiphase-boundary energies.
Interfacial short-range order governs deformation through its effect on the distribution of stacking-fault energies.
FCC/BCC interfaces act as pinning sites for dislocations.
Interface pinning promotes climb-assisted dislocation bypass under sustained load.
Short-range ordering raises local barriers to dislocation nucleation or motion.
Short-range ordering directs the spatial pattern of dislocation activity.
The proposed interface- and SRO-mediated process produces sustained plastic flow rather than rapid failure.
The proposed process prevents creep from being governed purely by dislocation glide.
In situ measurements will reveal gradual accumulation of climbing dislocations along and across interfaces.
Accumulated interfacial dislocations will form stable, partially pinned networks.
Greater interfacial short-range order will produce a more pronounced climb-induced creep regime.
Greater interfacial short-range order will reduce the creep strain rate.
Multilayers with little short-range order or fewer interfaces will exhibit less interface-mediated dislocation climb.
Multilayers with little short-range order or fewer interfaces will deform more through conventional dislocation glide.
Multilayers with little short-range order or fewer interfaces will have faster creep rates.
Multilayers with little short-range order or fewer interfaces will have reduced creep life.
The proposed mechanism operates primarily at temperatures and loading durations for which diffusion and dislocation climb are viable.
